inference_metadata.raw_response:

Explanation:
The video clip demonstrates the very beginning of an abdominal ultrasound exam. Initially, the image is dark and obscured as the probe is placed. The clinician then manipulates the probe to find an acoustic window, bringing the liver parenchyma into view. The probe is oriented transversely (cross-sectional), scanning across the liver to obtain a general survey of the organ's echotexture and vasculature before focusing on specific structures. This corresponds to establishing an initial window and performing a survey scan.

B. Track the inferior vena cava cranially to find the hepatic vein confluence into the IVC as the endpoint

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: D. Track the branch extending from the central landmark level to locate the gallbladder at its end

Explanation:
The video demonstrates the "main lobar fissure" (MLF) strategy. The operator identifies the main portal vein at the porta hepatis and then follows the hyperechoic line of the main lobar fissure (the "branch") which extends from the right portal vein/gallbladder neck area. By tracking this bright, linear structure, the probe is guided directly to the gallbladder fossa, revealing the gallbladder as the endpoint of the scan. This is a classic landmark technique for locating the gallbladder when it is difficult to find.

In contrast, the hepatic veins have thin, imperceptible walls that blend into the surrounding liver parenchyma. This is the classic B-mode visual distinction between these two vascular systems without using Doppler.
